blocks.x: This is Rio 1. Could we get your name on here first?
Yeah, Benji White is the name.
Let's see, today is March the...
16th.
1961. 1961. And we're at 103 Maryland Drive.
Right.
It's your home. Well, I might as well do this. I have this card here, which is a certificate of copyright registration for Owl Suit. This is by Wilfred B. White.
That's right. That's my full name.
Full name. And Harry, F-E-R-R-E-R.
Harry Farrell, or we used to call him Moe's. Moe's Farrell. He was a piano player at the time with the Owls.
And it's at 2216 Pond Street, New Orleans, Louisiana.
Yeah, that's where I lived at that time.

And the title of the music is Owl's Who, composed by E.H. Farrell and W.B. White of the United States, arranged by Owl Orchestra. Copy deposited, Maladine. Copy received, December the 31st, 1925. And the number is 629540.
That's right.
So that was, copyright was sent in about the time of the recording.

Just about the time of the recording. We had to send it in a little prior to the recording, as I recall, because they wouldn't record it unless it was copyrighted. And that was one of our first recordings. That together with a piece called Oh Me, Oh My, which none of us had written, but was just a sheet of music that we happened to have and were playing at that time. And that was our very, very first recordings, which were made here in New Orleans in the old Godshaw Building. They came down here, I think, from Atlanta. Columbia Recording sent people down here from Atlanta. And we went up to the Godshaw Building to make these recordings. It was quite an event for us at that time, I'll say. We enjoyed it very much. And, of course, now it sounds more or less just like the old-time recordings. I don't think their electronic recordings were at it best at that time. As I recall, that was some of the first electronic recordings that were made.
You were telling us about some trouble you had with the recording.

Well, when we made the recording, as I recall, they played it back principally to find out if we were seated right, to see whether the balance between the various instruments was correct. When they played it back, the predominant sound that came from the record was the baseball scores, which were being broadcast by WSMB at that time. Of course, that altered everything. They had to go to work and see if they could get that out of there, which they did. And then we made another trial run. And when they played that back, I'd say the thing that overpowered the music more than anything else was the stomping of our feet. And after we all removed our shoes and cushioned that, then we got the recording across. And it finally came out as, I think, as they expected it to, or hoped it would anyway.
We'd better go back to the beginning and start at the beginning of your life. The embarrassing question. When is your birth date?
When is it? When is it?
Mm-hmm.
It's on August the 30th. You mean when I was born?
Yes, the year.
1901. 1901. It's a long while ago. 59 years ago.
And were you born in the city?
Yeah, born right here in New Orleans.
What section of town?

I was born originally on First Street. And we moved from there to Valmont. We moved many times, various locations. Of course, Pine Street was the... I was actually, as a boy, I can recall my life on Calhoun, 1467 Calhoun Street, which was quite a neighborhood for young boys. We had, I guess, about 25 youngsters, all about the same age, within a radius of two city blocks there. We went to LaSalle Grammar School. I'd rather LaSalle... Yeah, the Grammar School. And then, of course, when high school came in, most of us were lost. Well, our friendship was split up, because I went to Newman Manual Training as part of my high school, and then went up east to Williston in East Hampton, Massachusetts, to complete my high school studies. Finally wound up with two years at Tulane University here in New Orleans. In the College of Commerce and Business Administration, I believe it was right at the beginning of the Business Administration. I know my uncle was one of the... Well, anyway, they called on certain business houses to sort of underwrite the College of Commerce and Business Administration when it first started, and he was one of those that was in that original group that underwrote that college. Yeah, old Dean Aldrich was a dean at that time. I remember going before him many times, because I wasn't the most brilliant student in the College of Commerce and Business Administration. We did a little playing while we were at Tulane. We had a little orchestra up there. It was more fun than anything else. Had no idea of playing professionally at all. That, our idea of playing professionally... Rather, we never had an idea of playing professionally, but we used to get together. Funny thing, there was a band here, not a band, but a string outfit called the Six and Seven Eights, if you recall, which Dr. Sushong was just on This Is Your Life, as you recall. And some of our boys who were with us were in that. For instance, Red Mackey was one of them that was with the Six and Seven Eights. Eblen Rowe was one that was with the Six and Seven Eights. Monk Smith, who is now dead, was with the Six and Seven Eights. Well, at the same time, we had a little string outfit. Originally, I played violin. And we were playing on the... We had a summer vacation on the Gulf Coast. We played three days a week at the Miramar Hotel and passed Christiane, and three days a week at the Belmar Hotel in Mississippi City, I think that's what it was, between Gulfport and Biloxi. A fellow by the name of McLaughrey, as I understand, owned it at that time. And there was a chap here in New Orleans who got this engagement by the name of Guy Lyman. He's passed away now. He couldn't play any instruments, but he loved to play drums. But he didn't even own a set of drums. He had nothing but just an ordinary crate with a bunch of cans and things hooked on it. Believe it or not, there were... Let's see, there was Eugene DeBall, or Jinx as we call him, Jinx DeBall. There was a fellow by the name of Fred Ogden. There was Eblen Rowe, Guy Lyman, and me. And we went over this summer to play at these two hotels. And that was our first experience in the professional end of music. It was really a holiday for us, we enjoyed it immensely. And that's where I started playing saxophone. We used to go down to Biloxi and listen to the band at the Hotel Biloxi, and they had a saxophone player in there who I thought was very good. So one weekend I came back to New Orleans and went to one of the huck shops here and bought a saxophone. Went over to Whirlines and bought a new mouthpiece for it. I didn't know who'd been blowing it. And took it back over the Gulf Coast with me and started blowing that thing. And boy, I never got so much razzing in all my life. Got old socks and everything else put in it that quieted me down. Finally, I learned how to play the thing. Well, our summer over there was a rather nice vacation. And we came back. And then we started playing some of the group. Eblen Rowe, Monk Smith, came out of the 6 and 7 8s. And Rene Jalpe, and I, I don't recall some of the others, but we used to play on weekends out at West End at what was then known as the Agnes Boathouse. It was in the pen where they keep these yachts. The name of Daddy McKnight, as I recall, owned that. And we used to go out there every Saturday night and just play for our own benefit. We'd have a good time out there. And from that, Red Mackey and his brother, Dick Mackey, who played the cornet. Red played the, was playing the bass with the 6 and 7 8s, but he also played piano. There was Red Mackey and Dick Mackey, his brother, Monk Smith, who played the saxophone at that time. Rene Jalpe, who played banjo. And I got together to form a little, a little band. And we played for a subscription dance, as I recall it, down at the old Courtshade Club, down in the French Quarter. We didn't make any money, but we had a lot of fun. And from there, we played one or two engagements, started to play a few engagements, at the old rowing club, which used to be out at the end of the, out at the, Biosync John here. They had regular dances out there, which we played for. And then, I recall one incident, and I don't recall, I'm not sure of the name of the girl, I'm, I know her very well, but I'm not too positive about it, so I don't want to mention her name. But anyway, she was the debutante of the year. And she had a debutante party. And she asked us if we'd mind playing for the debutante party. And we told them, no, we wouldn't mind. So we went to play for this debutante party. And she had engaged Guy Lyman's orchestra, who was here on the Orphium Circuit at that time. He was playing at the Orphium Circuit. Well, he came out to the country club, New Orleans Country Club. And we were there, and we put our instruments down, and went, sat down with the rest of the guests, because we're all personal friends of them. And he wanted to know, how we rated, uh, eating with the rest of the guests. Well, we weren't out there playing, for, professionally, we were out there enjoying ourselves. It was quite a party. But from then on, we began to get engagements of spot jobbing around at various places, and, and began to actually sell the band. Then, I never will forget, one day, we went down to the Roosevelt Hotel, Earl Crone, who was drummer at the time, with us, and I went down there. I don't know, I can't, I really don't know why we went down, but we went down to see about playing in the, what was then, the Venetian Room. And we talked to the manager, whose name was Weber, and he said, well, fine, come on, we'll start right away. You fellas got a nice following, so we went to work in the, in the Venetian Room. And we'd play all winter long in the Venetian Room. When that was over, we'd go in the summer, out to the West End Roof Garden, and we played, if, I hope I'm correcting this, about four seasons, alternating between the Venetian Room, and the, and the West End Roof Garden. We had a marvelous, time along, because it was all a big happy event with us. We were just a bunch of school kids, having a, a big time. Hi guys. I'll never forget one night, we were on the West End Roof Garden, and, this chap, by the name of, now what is his name, he owned this big, home out here in City Park. Um, I can't think of his name, I was a big oil man here. Anyway, he called up the West End Roof Garden, wanted to know if they had a big crowd out there, and he said, no, we don't have too many, and I said, we'll close it up. I want the band out at my home, in City Park, he was throwing a party. So they closed up the West End Roof Garden that night, and we went out and played all night long, till six o'clock in the morning, and then left there, and went from there out to the, because another one of the guests, who was,
at,

at this party, was having a Cafe Bulo party, at Tranchinas, which was at, Millenburg, at that, or Spanish Fort. We went out there, and played till about ten o'clock, that next day, it was one of the most rugged nights, we ever had in our lives. But we had some wonderful times, playing on that West End Roof Garden. One of the things, that was so enjoyable about it, we used to go out every afternoon, at two o'clock, and rehearse. A lot of the girls from Newcomb, would come out there, to listen to us rehearse. Being all single boys, and some of them that were, thinking about college, and so forth, half the band would be, rehearsing one, one number, the other half dancing, and then the other half would, rehearse, and the other half would dance. So we really enjoyed our work, I'll tell you that. And I just don't recall, how this recording started, I don't recall, but we were contacted, by the Columbia Recording Company, to make a record. And as I understand it, as I remember it, they wanted an original number. And that's how the Owl's Hoot, came into being, along with Oh Me, Oh My, which was not an original number. And those were the first two, that we recorded. And about, I think it was two years later, we were packed up, and sent to Atlanta, where we made all the rest, of these recordings that we have. I think there's a total, of 15 recordings, all together. But those recordings, were, except for, Eccentric, and West End Romp, were music, that was sent to us, by the, by the Columbia Recording Company, and we were told, that was what we were to play. Frankly, I don't like any of them, except the, Eccentric, and the few that we, we were just ad-libbing, and playing that way. But, we played them, I don't think they ever, any of them ever went over too well, although, there's an awful lot of talk about them, still going on, and occasionally we hear them on the radio, when they talk about old timers. But you know, it's a funny thing, when we started playing, there were very, very few, uh, uh, white bands, in existence. Most all of them, and the good jazz bands, were really colored, colored jazz bands. And, it was a little, it was a peculiar feeling, for us to break into this, uh, jazz field here, uh, under those conditions. Now, you want to rub that out, you can rub,
no, no, I mean,

rub it out, but, that was a fact. And, uh, it was, because, uh, except for the fact, that most of us, had been, had even, had a year of college or so, and were, pretty well known in New Orleans, uh, you take, most of those boys, that were with us, were, from excellent families, and, didn't consider it a livelihood, they considered it, a lark, is what they did, but the thing got control, and it became a livelihood, with us, for quite a number of years. And then, well, to get back to the whole history, the Owls, after, after we, we played the, the Roosfelt, then we went to, uh, we, went to the, uh, well, we played, first of all, we played on the Strand Theater, as you know, we won that contest, and played on the Strand Theater, uh, for a week, then we, went to the Roosfelt, we left the Roosfelt, we didn't leave then, but we went on the, on the Orpheum, stage, for a week, I don't know how we got on there, frankly, I don't remember what the circumstances were, that got us on there,
but we were on there.

Then we left there, and went to Victory Inn, played at Victory Inn, for, uh, quite a little time, and we left there, and went to, uh, to the, uh, Edgewater Gulf Hotel, in, uh, in Black Sea, we opened that hotel up, we opened up also another hotel, in, in Gulfport, because we didn't play there, we only played there the opening night, and, uh, I can't think of the name of that hotel, but anyway, we,
Was it near the Markham Hotel, in that area?

It was the Markham Hotel, we opened that up, the new Markham Hotel, in our barnstorming days, uh, when we were playing with the Strand Theater, this is quite an incident, uh, we, uh, had a tour during the summertime, went all up through the country, up into North Louisiana, Mississippi, even up to Arkansas, uh, playing, playing, one night stands, in various theaters, and we got to a place, called, uh, let's see, it was up here in Arkansas, uh, well anyway, we played a theater there, and we were supposed, supposed to play a dance, the same night, the two dates were, the two times were conflicting, and, I didn't know whether we'd get out of there, safely or not, but we finally managed to play both of the engagements, and then we had an engagement to play in a town called Smackover, Arkansas, and, when we got through playing the dance, went to the hotel, we asked the fellow how far Smackover was, he said it was 15 or 18 miles, said, well we thought we'd ride it at night, he said, I wouldn't do that if I were you, he said, they hold him up every night between here and Smackover, and he says, if they don't have anything on him, tell him to go back and get it, he said, I don't think you fellas ought to ride up there during the night, so we waited until the next day, and then we got into Smackover, and Smackover was the funniest town I've ever gone into in my life, I'll tell you, it was an oil town, it was a boom town in those days, and that's a long time ago, it was right in the middle of Prohibition, in the middle of the street as we drove in, they had an enormous beer barrel up there, whether it had beer in it or not, I don't know, but it was the most rough and tumble town I've ever been in my life, and we were supposed to open a country club there, and this country club was, opening of the country club was supposed to be a, a dance where they paid so much admission, and we were supposed to get a percentage of the admission, we later found out that it was strictly a membership deal, and only so many people were allowed to come, and we couldn't possibly make any money out of it, no matter, if everybody came, it was supposed to come, but we got out of there, and got back safely, and that was before we went into the Roosevelt, and to get back after we finally, we left the Edgewater Gulf Hotel, we came back, and we went out to what was called the Halfway House, remember the Halfway House here, it's still out there now, but I think it's, it's Orkins now, or some such place, I think Brunus had been playing in there before we were, and we took that place over, and played out there for quite a while, and then, some of the boys in the orchestra, like Rainier Jalpe, and Siegfried Christensen, who was a pianist, he was a young chap, they decided they were going back, to complete their college education, that they'd had, as much as they wanted of music, they'd made a little money, that would get them through college, and they did, they went back, Rainier went back, and completed his education, as an architect, and Sieg Christensen, who was a married man at that time, went back and became a lawyer, and he's a lawyer in town today, and it was right after that, that the, the bands broke up, we all went, I got married, and went into business, my wife said, if you're going to play music, you're not going to marry me, because I don't want you to run around, all the country every night, so we broke up at that time, some of the boys went on, to play, at, suburban gardens, I think it was, Earl Crumb, and a few of the others, but it's very interesting, some of the chaps, that are in the, big time now, that have played with us, on various occasions, either as substitutes, or as, well, part-time fellows, that were with us, for, Eddie Miller for one, when we were at the Owl's Nest, as we'd call it, Eddie Miller was with us, as, as a saxophonist, at that time, Eddie went on, to be with, one of the, top notches, Nappy Lamar, I don't know whether, you ever heard of Nappy Lamar, he is, he is now out in Hollywood, I think, played, guitar with us, and made a recording with us, the Owls, the, the, the, Throwing the Horns, record was made, with Nappy Lamar, in, in there.
What did he do on that record, did he play banjo, or guitar?

He played guitar, and he, and Pinky Vedakovich, sang a, a little solo, if you'll notice, on the record. Then another one, that played with us, was, oh, what was that fellow's name? Alfred Galladora. I don't know whether you know, Alfred Galladora, but he played, oh, two or three occasions, with us, at the Southern Yacht Club, when we were spotting. And that was as fine a musician, as I ever, bump up the gifts in my life. I've never met a musician, that could, could transpose, any piece of music, that you put up in front of him, and read it off on that saxophone, like that fellow could. He just, he made me feel so insignificant, as a saxophone player, that I realized, right then and there, that it was time for me, to get out of the music business. They had men like that in it, knew what they were doing, and were, in such control of music. And he was, he was a very, very fine musician. All in all, it's been a very, very comfortable, I wouldn't have missed it, for anything in the world. I think if I had it to do over again, I'd do the same thing. Fact is, if I had it to do over again, I might have stayed in music, because I enjoyed it, so much more than anything, I've ever done in my life. I don't play anymore, I've got the horns, but I don't play anymore. It's a funny thing, but neither one of my youngsters have been too particularly interested in learning music. I think they would have liked to have played, but they didn't want to put the effort in it to learn how to play. But it's been very, very enlightening to me, and it's been the friends that I made through playing music. To give you a little instance of that, when we played at the roof garden, we used to meet so many people, and so many people would call me by name, and I'm a very poor individual in remembering names. So I made up my mind one night, I told Monk, I said, Monk, I can't remember these people's names, and I said, I just insult them when I say hi. I said, I'm going to start something here that I hope will get me out of this dilemma I'm in. I said, I'm going to call everybody Joe. Then if I say hi Joe, they'll say, well, that's all right, he calls everybody Joe. He knows who I am, but he calls me Joe, and that's what I did. For years and years, I called everybody Joe. My best friend was Joe to me, simply for one reason, that I met so many people through music, and I could not remember their names. I just couldn't do it. I didn't want to insult them by calling them, just say hi there, so I started calling everybody Joe. Men, women, and children, all alike, were called Joe. It got me out of an awful predicament that I was in. Later on in life, when I went back into the jewelry business, one of the gentlemen that was there, I called him Joe, he called me Joe, and people used to say, I don't understand why you two fellas got together, and both of your names are Joe. But, well, I guess there's a lot of other experiences that I could relate, if I could only think of them. I know, you know.
Well, to get back to the very beginning, were your family musical before you?

No. Nobody in my family played a musical instrument. I started in, I studied the violin. I actually studied violin for seven years. But I never could play the thing worth a nickel. I learned music, but I never could play the violin. I used to, one of, my main trouble was I wouldn't read music. I'd play the violin all right, but everything I was playing was being played by ear. And when Professor Shank, or Shrank, would come up to hear my lessons, he'd tell me point blank, you're playing by ear, you're not reading those music. And I'd tell him, yeah, that's a fact, I am playing by ear. I played the violin, as I said, the only time I ever played the violin was in that summer that we spent it across the lake when I became interested in the saxophone. And I picked that up without studying it.
How old were you when you started on violin?
Oh, on violin, I must have been about 16 years old. 15 or 16.
You started 15 or 16. Yeah. And, let's see, you took up saxophone when you were over there? How old were you when you crossed the lake?
Well, I must have been about 19 years old. That's,
that's about how old I was
when we were playing on the Gulf Coast.
So you were playing professionally in 1920 then?
Oh yeah.
Oh yeah. Oh, that Ogden fellow, I didn't get what instrument he played over there.
He played banjo. Fred Ogden.
So you had a banjo and a drum.
We had, it was a funny thing, we had a banjo, a guitar, two violins, and Guy Lyman on this contraption he had, it wasn't a drum, it was just a box with a bunch of plates on it that he would beat on.
Who was the guitar player again? Was that Mark Smith?
No, no, no, that wasn't. That was Jinx DeBall or Eugene DeBall.
Oh yeah.

He's a, I think he's an architect here in town now. And Ogden was with the Bonds Department of one of the banks, I haven't seen him in years so I don't know what he's doing now. and Ogden was, was, well he wrote some of the funniest little pieces of music with words to it that, they were just cute pieces that's all and that was, as we used those to entertain the people at these two hotels over there. That was a forerunner to the, to the Owls. The original Owls was composed, the actual original Owls was composed of, of the two Mackey boys Red Mackey, Dick Mackey, Monk Smith, Eblin Rao, and myself. That was the original, original Owls. Later, Moe's fair came in on the piano and Red Mackey went to the bass and later, Moe's, well Moe's was with us at the Roosevelt Hotel but then we brought in another piano player called, Sig Christiansen, who made, quite a few of these recordings with us. A fellow, another trumpet player came with us too was Red Bowman, who was with us for a while. The original Owls were those five that I named and then of course we, when we got into the Roosevelt Hotel, Pinky came in, Dan LeBlanc came in on the bass and, well, Billy Burton came in as a, a leader. He wasn't with us so more than just a few months. Just a few months.
You had a song on too.
Oh, that, well, that was,
yeah, that was, um, um,

A trombone player's name that we were trying to think of a minute ago was, well now we can't think of it. Frank Netto. Frank Netto. That's right. I see Frank quite frequently and enjoy his playing so much he's still playing. Frank was a musician, a very fine musician. He played not only trombone but he played violin. He played almost any instrument. He was called upon to do it. I know when we were at the Edgewater Gulf Hotel we had to play a lot of this sweet music for dinner music and he used to put the trombone down and pick up the violin because we had to have a leader that was just supposed to be there, that's all.
Oh Ebby Rao, you're saying you were playing at that chess club?

Chess Checker and Whisk Club. We had a picture there, it was a masquerade party, it was quite a picture. Boy, that goes back a long time. But Ebby played with us all the while we were spotting, spot jobbing. Ebby played with us.
